title: Why we sometimes need to chain atoms together
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton describes a coaching observation in which atomisation, breaking a routine into its smallest teachable parts, failed. A teacher confirmed that students were secure on each prerequisite atom for filling in a table of values, yet they fell apart the moment the full routine combined those atoms. Barton hypothesises that the leap from isolated atoms to the whole multi-step process was too large, and he takes responsibility because he had delivered the original CPD on atomisation. His fix is to chain two or three atoms together first, such as multiplying and then adding with negatives, and only add further atoms once that chain is secure. The piece is a short, honest refinement of a technique rather than a rejection of it.
points: Mastering atoms one at a time does not guarantee students can combine them, so the jump to the full routine needs a bridge.
Barton's remedy is incremental chaining: teach or assess two or three atoms, secure the chain, then add more atoms.
The worked case (plotting straight-line graphs from a table of values) shows how negative-number arithmetic can collapse once students must also interpret expressions and substitute.
The post models a useful coaching stance: owning a mistake in advice previously given.
quotes: I define Atomisation as breaking routines down into their smallest constituent parts (atoms) that can be assessed or taught separately from the routine itself

The teacher assessed each of the atoms with well-chosen questions, and students were able to answer them successfully. So, he moved on to the new routine – filling in a table of values – which used each of these atoms.
Suddenly, 2 x (-3) = 6, or (-6) + 2 = -8, despite no students making these mistakes some 30 seconds before.

We hypothesised that the jump from answering questions on individual atoms to carrying out a process involving these atoms combined (interpreting algebraic expressions, substituting, multiplying negative numbers, and adding negative numbers) was too much for these students.
Students could then have focused on these two atoms without extra attention needing to be diverted towards thinking about the other atoms, such as interpreting expressions and substitution.

If there are several atoms, then a more sensible approach is to teach or assess two or three atoms individually and then chain those together. Once students are secure with that chain, teach or assess more atoms and add those to the chain.
